item.title: China-linked hackers exploit Google Calendar in cyberattacks on governments
item.description:
Source: The Record


A China-based hacking group abused Google Calendar in a new cyber-espionage campaign targeting government entities, researchers have found. In a report released this week, analysts at Google attributed the campaign to APT41 — also tracked as Brass Typhoon, Wicked Panda and RedGolf — a long-running state-backed operation. The group’s primary targets include foreign governments and organizations in sectors such as logistics, media, automobiles and technology. Google noted that the abuse of legitimate cloud services like Google Calendar allows attackers to blend in with normal traffic, making detection more difficult. Full Story

item.title: ConnectWise Hit by Cyberattack; Nation-State Actor Suspected in Breach
item.description:
Source: The Hacker News


Tampa, Fla.-based ConnectWise, the developer of remote access and support software ScreenConnect, disclosed in a May 28 advisory that it was the victim of a cyberattack likely perpetrated by a nation-state threat actor. The company engaged Google Mandiant to conduct a forensic probe into the incident, which was first reported by CRN. It did not reveal the exact number of customers who were impacted by the hack, when it happened, or the identity of the threat actor behind it, and said it has implemented enhanced monitoring and hardening measures across its environment to prevent such attacks from happening again in the future. ConnectWise is used by 100,000 managed service provider (MSP) and IT professionals. Full Story

item.title: 184M Passwords Exposed In Leak Affecting Apple And Google Users
item.description:
Source: New York Post


More than 184 million passwords may have been exposed in a massive data breach that experts are calling a “cybercriminal’s dream.” The leak appears to have affected everything from Apple and Google usernames and passwords and social media logins to bank accounts. The database containing the compromised passwords was unencrypted and not password-protected itself, according to a researcher claiming to have made the discovery. CNET reports that the database has been removed from public access and that a percentage of the login credentials in the 47.5 gigabyte file are likely outdated. Full Story

item.title: Man who stole 1,000 DVDs from employer strikes plea deal over movie leaks
item.description:
Source: ars TECHNICA


An accused movie pirate who stole more than 1,000 Blu-ray discs and DVDs while working for a DVD manufacturing company struck a plea deal this week to lower his sentence after the FBI claimed the man's piracy cost movie studios millions. Steven Hale no longer works for the DVD company. He was arrested in March, accused of "bypassing encryption that prevents unauthorized copying" and ripping pre-release copies of movies he could only access because his former employer was used by major movie studios. Among the popular movies that Hale is believed to have leaked between 2021 and 2022 was Spider-Man: No Way Home, which the FBI alleged was copied tens of millions of times. Full Story

item.title: Cybercrime To Cost The World $12.2 Trillion Annually By 2031
item.description:
Source: Associated Press


Cybercrime is predicted to cost the world $10.5 trillion USD in 2025, according to the '2025 Official Cybercrime Report' from Cybersecurity Ventures. If it were measured as a country, then cybercrime would be the world’s third largest economy after the U.S. and China. Global cybercriminal activity has grown so large that, after years of rapid expansion, Cybersecurity Ventures believes the sector’s sheer economic weight will see growth plateau at 2.5 percent annually through 2031, at which point cybercrime will cost the world $12.2 trillion annually. Press Release

item.title: Ransomware hits Singapore-based data handling firm
item.description:
Source: Channel News Asia (CNA)


A ransomware attack on a Singapore-based data handling service provider has compromised the personal information of at least 146 Income Insurance policy holders. The company in question, DataPost, is in the early stages of investigating the attack, the firm said May 29. DataPost was responsible for the printing and mailing of some of Income Insurance policy holders' documents, the insurer said in a separate statement, adding that affected customers' bonus statements had been compromised. DataPost, which works with government agencies and financial institutions, among others, told CNA its investigations "will take time to complete". Full Story

item.title: Britain is set to splash £1billion on an 'army of hackers' to target the likes of Putin
item.description:
Source: DailyMail.com


The British military is looking to throw a massive £1billion into AI and what's been dubbed an army of hackers. The Defence Secretary says the Government has plans to set up a cyber command to counter a 'continual and intensifying' level of cyber warfare as part of the strategic defence review. This will help protect the U.K., and give the country the option to unleash such 'teams' on the likes of Russia. Defence Secretary John Healey said Government will also invest more than £1billion into a new 'digital targeting web' to be set up by 2027. Full Story

item.title: Victoria’s Secret takes down its website after a security incident
item.description:
Source: CNN


Shares of Victoria’s Secret fell May 28 after the lingerie company took down its U.S. website, saying there was a prolonged “security incident.” The retailer has “identified and are taking steps to address a security incident,” according to a statement posted to its website. “We have taken down our website and some in-store services as a precaution.” A report from Bloomberg and posts on social media indicate the outage has been going on since at least May 26. While its physical retail stores remain open, revenue from online shopping is critical for Victoria’s Secret. The brand generated $2 billion in net sales from direct channels that include online shopping in 2024, or roughly a third of its annual sales. Full Story

item.title: Data broker giant LexisNexis says breach exposed personal information of over 364,000 people
item.description:
Source: TechCrunch


LexisNexis Risk Solutions, a data broker that collects and uses consumers’ personal data to help its paying corporate customers detect possible risk and fraud, has disclosed a data breach affecting more than 364,000 people. The company said in a filing with Maine’s attorney general that the breach, dating back to Dec. 25, 2024, allowed a hacker to obtain consumers’ sensitive personal data from a third-party platform used by the company for software development. A spokesperson for LexisNexis told TechCrunch that an unknown hacker accessed the company’s GitHub account. The stolen data varies, but includes names, dates of birth, phone numbers, postal and email addresses, Social Security numbers, and driver license numbers. Full Story

item.title: Cyberattack Hit South Jersey's Largest Healthcare System
item.description:
Source: NJBIZ


A cyberattack on Cooper University Health Care last year may have exposed the data of nearly 60,000 current and former patients, according to the Camden-based health care system. After detecting unusual activity on its network in May 2024, Cooper “immediately” took steps to secure its systems and launched an investigation, it said in an alert posted online. Cooper said it completed its investigation Mar. 26, 2025. As South Jersey’s largest health care system, Cooper’s footprint spans three hospitals, six urgent care centers and more than 130 outpatient officers. Full Story

item.title: Estonia issues arrest warrant for Moroccan wanted for major pharmacy data breach
item.description:
Source: The Record


Estonian authorities have launched an international search for a Moroccan citizen suspected in one of the country’s largest data breaches, which exposed sensitive customer data from a popular pharmacy chain. 25-year-old Adrar Khalid is suspected of unlawfully accessing a customer card database managed by Allium UPI, the parent company of the Apotheka pharmacy chain, in Feb. 2024. Investigators believe he logged into the system using administrator credentials, though how he obtained the password remains under investigation. According to previous reports, the breach exposed nearly 700,000 personal identification codes, over 400,000 email addresses, nearly 60,000 home addresses and about 30,000 phone numbers. Full Story

item.title: Apple Blocks $9 Billion in Fraud Over 5 Years Amid Rising App Store Threats
item.description:
Source: The Hacker News


Apple on May 27 revealed that it prevented over $9 billion in fraudulent transactions in the last five years, including more than $2 billion in 2024 alone. The company said the App Store is confronted by a wide range of threats that seek to defraud users in various ways, ranging from "deceptive apps designed to steal personal information to fraudulent payment schemes that attempt to exploit users." The tech giant said it terminated more than 46,000 developer accounts over fraud concerns and rejected an additional 139,000 developer enrollment as part of efforts to prevent bad actors from submitting their apps to the App Store. Full Story

item.title: Second Suspect Surrenders in Alleged New York Crypto Kidnapping Case
item.description:
Source: The Wall Street Journal


Two crypto investors face kidnapping charges for allegedly holding a wealthy trader captive in a New York City townhouse for three weeks for his bitcoin, law-enforcement officials said. John Woeltz, 37 years old, was arraigned May 24 in a state court in Manhattan on five counts, including kidnapping, assault and unlawful imprisonment, for allegedly tying up and torturing the victim in hopes of obtaining the password to the man’s crypto account, according to a criminal complaint. William Duplessie, an alleged accomplice of Woeltz, surrendered to police on May 27, according to New York Police Department Commissioner Jessica Tisch. Duplessie is the former chief executive of a Swiss crypto investment firm, records show. Full Story

item.title: Prague accuses China of hacking Czech foreign ministry
item.description:
Source: Politico


The Czech government May 27 condemned China for carrying out a cyberattack against its foreign ministry exposing thousands of unclassified emails. Czechia said that the Chinese state-sponsored group Advanced Persistent Threat 31 (APT31) targeted the foreign ministry from 2022 — the year the country held the rotating EU presidency — and was able to read unclassified emails sent between embassies and EU institutions. The Czech foreign minister, Jan Lipavský, said he would summon the Chinese ambassador immediately to explain the findings and tell him this would damage the countries' bilateral relations. The alleged Chinese hack sparked outrage in Brussels, among the EU's top brass and at NATO headquarters. Full Story

item.title: Hacker who crippled Baltimore in 2019 ransomware attack pleads guilty
item.description:
Source: The Baltimore Banner


An Iranian man has pleaded guilty for his role in a ransomware attack that crippled Baltimore’s computer network in 2019, halting critical city services and costing more than $19 million. Sina Gholinejad entered the plea May 27, admitting his role in the scheme that took hostage computer networks of several cities, corporations and health care organizations. Once Gholinejad and his unnamed co-conspirators accessed the networks, they encrypted files and extorted Bitcoin payments via a variant of ransomware known as Robbinhood, according to a news release from the U.S. Department of Justice. Gholinejad is scheduled to be sentenced in August. Full Story

item.title: Dutch intelligence agencies say Russian hackers stole police data in cyberattack
item.description:
Source: Reuters


A previously unknown Russian hacker group with suspected ties to the Kremlin was responsible for a cyberattack last year on the Dutch police and has also targeted other Western nations that deliver military support to Ukraine, intelligence agencies announced May 27. The agencies said in a report that the group, which they called Laundry Bear, is actively trying to steal sensitive data from European Union and NATO countries and is “extremely likely Russian state supported.” The Russian hackers broke into a police account and accessed work-related contact details of all Dutch police officers in Sep. 2024, in a cyberattack that sent shockwaves through the force. Full Story

item.title: RE/MAX deals with alleged 150GB data theft: Medusa ransomware demands $200K
item.description:
Source: Cybernews


RE/MAX, an international real estate network with over 9000 offices worldwide, has been allegedly breached by Medusa ransomware, a major threat actor targeting large organizations. Medusa released samples of files and demanded a $200,000 ransom for the erasure of the remaining 150GB. The breach is not yet officially confirmed. On May 27, Medusa Ransomware posted RE/MAX on its leak site on the dark web, claiming it had exfiltrated 150GB of data. A countdown timer leaves less than 18 days to pay up before the data is released publicly. The available data doesn’t appear to be super sensitive or valuable, according to a Cybernews researcher, but the sample is small, and the rest of the leak might contain more sensitive data. Full Story

item.title: MathWorks bringing systems back online following ransomware attack
item.description:
Source: The Record


The developer of the popular MATLAB programming language and numeric computing environment said a ransomware attack is impacting its IT systems. Natick, Mass.-based MathWorks provided an update to customers May 26 after initially reporting outages May 18, confirming that it experienced a ransomware attack that took down online applications and internal systems used by staff. MathWorks has millions of users, many of which are engineers and scientists who use MATLAB for data analysis, computation and more. MATLAB and other MathWorks products are used by about 6,500 colleges and universities, according to the company. The company has 6,500 employees and more than 30 offices across Europe, Asia and North America. Full Story

item.title: Everest Ransomware Leaks Coca-Cola Employee Data Online
item.description:
Source: HackRead


HackRead reports the Everest ransomware group claimed responsibility for stealing data on 959 Coca-Cola employees across the Middle East, including the UAE, Oman, and Bahrain. Everest leaked sensitive employee data on its dark web site as well as on the notorious Russian-language cybercrime forum XSS. The group has posted a 502 megabyte data dump. The leaked folder contains 1,104 files with information that includes: Full names of employees; Business and home addresses; Family and marriage certificates; Copies of visas, passports, residency permits; Phone numbers, banking details, salary records; and Employee email addresses. Separately, another hacker group claimed to have stolen 23 million records from Coca-Cola Europacific Partners (CCEP). Full Story

item.title: Solana co-founder's personal info leaked on Migos' Instagram in suspected data breach
item.description:
Source: Crypto Briefing


The official Instagram account of hip-hop group Migos was hacked May 26, with the page briefly turning into a leaked site for sensitive personal information belonging to Solana co-founder Raj Gokal. According to "Andy" on X, co-founder of The Rollup, the compromised account, which has over 13 million followers, posted a series of photos of alleged IDs, passport scans, and other private data linked to Gokal and another individual identified as “Arvind.” The leaked docs were paired with threatening captions and explicit references to an unpaid crypto ransom, including one post stating, “you should’ve paid the 40 btc,” indicating a failed extortion effort. The hackers also modified the account’s bio to promote a meme coin scam and shared Telegram links and audio files. Full Story
